title: Musical Taste, Beauty, and Love for God
author: Brian Pell
summary: Beauty is not subjective but an encounter with God's objective glory, yet our finite limitations and the kaleidoscopic array of human experience mean we perceive beauty through different vantage points. Pell argues against legalistic restriction of musical taste (his childhood experience) and instead proposes a framework centered on love, community, intention, and religion. The piece moves through how Christians should cultivate beauty through deliberate engagement while resisting consumer culture's brain-chemistry hijacking, sharing aesthetic experiences in community, and understanding our musical preferences as expressions of worship and encounters with the divine. Ultimately, Pell contends that when we pursue beauty rightly, we are pursuing relationship with God.
points: Beauty is objective (rooted in God's glory), yet its expression is kaleidoscopic because we are finite beings who encounter it through different stories, emotions, and limitations, not because beauty itself is subjective.

Legalism around art forms damages faith more than it protects it; restricting what young people can enjoy aesthetically erodes trust in authority figures and drives a wedge between beauty and love of God.

Intentional, rhythmic engagement with beauty is essential because consumer culture floods us with distraction and addiction-forming entertainment that atrophies our capacity to perceive and cultivate beauty.

Beauty moves us most powerfully when it is shared in community and when our taste is connected to our love of others through the sacrificial work of adjusting what we enjoy for the sake of those we care for.

Religious practice gives anchor and meaning to aesthetic experience; beauty without a trajectory toward God becomes aimless awe, missing the main point that our chief end is to glorify and enjoy God forever.
